opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I try to be careful not to overstate it. If you look at DiT purely from a technical point of view, it isn't a very complicated idea. At that time, diffusion models were almost all built on U-Net, which came from the medical imaging and segmentation world. Meanwhile, in recognition and in language, everyone had already moved to Transformers. So the question Bill Peebles and I asked was very simple: can we take the U-Net away and just use a standard Transformer, operating on latent patches, and does it scale?

I think the real contribution is less about any single trick and more about showing a clean, scalable recipe. We showed that when you increase the compute, the Gflops, the image quality improves very predictably. That gives people confidence that this architecture can follow the same scaling path we saw in language models. It also unifies the architecture across modalities, which matters a lot for the field. Later, when Bill went to OpenAI and worked on Sora, that design philosophy carried over, and many video and image generation systems today are built on some variant of the diffusion Transformer. That was something we did not fully anticipate, and of course a lot of credit goes to the people who scaled it up.

SiT is a natural follow-up. DiT answered the architecture question, but the training framework was still the original diffusion formulation. With SiT, we used the interpolant framework, which connects diffusion and flow matching, to study the design space more systematically: how you interpolate between data and noise, whether you predict velocity or noise, whether you sample with an ODE or an SDE. We found that keeping the same backbone while making these choices more carefully gives consistent improvements. So I see SiT less as a brand-new idea and more as a way to clarify and modularize things, so people can understand which parts actually matter.

If I had to summarize, I think both works are about simplification and unification. In research, people often like to add components. Sometimes the more valuable thing is to remove unnecessary ones and show that a simple, general architecture can scale. That said, I don't think the story is finished. Diffusion Transformers are still quite separate from representation learning and from understanding models, and that is what I am most interested in now: how generation and understanding can really come together.

r001.rationale: The response says many later image and video generation systems use a DiT variant, but it does not characterize DiT and SiT as academic baselines for subsequent research.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think the contribution of DiT and SiT is simpler than people sometimes make it out to be. When we started DiT, the question we were asking was almost boring: does the U-Net actually matter for diffusion models, or is it just a historical artifact? Everyone in the field had inherited the U-Net from the early DDPM work, and nobody had really tested whether that inductive bias was doing anything. So we replaced it with a plain Transformer, and the main finding was that it works, and more importantly, that it scales. You could draw a clean line between compute and FID, and that line kept going.

I think that scaling result is the real contribution. Not the architecture itself, because frankly there is nothing clever in the architecture. It is a ViT with adaptive layer norm for conditioning. The contribution was removing a belief. Once people saw that you did not need the U-Net, the field could reuse all of the infrastructure, the scaling laws, the engineering knowledge that had been built up around Transformers for language. That is why you see DiT-style backbones in Sora, in Stable Diffusion 3, in Flux and so on. It was not that we invented something, it was that we simplified something so that it could be scaled.

SiT came from a similar instinct. With DiT we fixed the architecture and asked about scaling. With SiT we fixed the architecture and asked about the generative formulation itself. Diffusion, flow matching, stochastic interpolants, these were all floating around as somewhat separate camps, and we wanted a single framework where you could vary the interpolant, the prediction target, the sampler, and see what actually matters. The finding was that a lot of the design choices that people argued about were pretty interchangeable, but a few of them, like moving to a simpler linear interpolant and velocity prediction, gave a consistent improvement at the same compute. Again, it is a clarifying result more than an inventive one.

If I am being critical of my own work, I would say neither paper is a conceptual breakthrough. They are what I would call good science papers. They set up a clean controlled comparison and let the community stop arguing about certain things. In a field that moves this fast, I think that kind of work is undervalued. Everyone wants the new idea, but a lot of progress comes from somebody carefully showing which old ideas you can throw away. That is how I would judge them: DiT told people what architecture to stop worrying about, and SiT told people what formulation to stop worrying about. Then the real work of scaling and building products could go on without those distractions.

r001.rationale: The response says DiT-style backbones were adopted in later models and that both papers clarified design choices, but it does not characterize DiT and SiT as academic baselines for subsequent research.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate their contributions. DiT asks a fairly fundamental architectural question: can we replace the U-Net in diffusion models with a Transformer? The significance isn’t just that the replacement works. It gives us a relatively simple, scalable architecture and shows a clear relationship between more compute and better generation quality. That makes it a useful foundation for further work.

SiT takes that architecture and asks a different question: how much does the formulation of the generative process matter? It explores the interpolant connecting data and noise, the prediction objective, and the sampling procedure within a common framework. So you can improve generation without attributing every gain to a new network architecture.

To me, they’re complementary. DiT establishes a scalable backbone; SiT helps us understand how to train and sample models built on that backbone. I wouldn’t judge either solely by a benchmark number. I’d also ask whether it makes the next experiment simpler and opens up useful directions for other researchers.

r001.rationale: The response calls DiT a foundation and says SiT opens useful directions, but it does not characterize both as academic baselines on which subsequent research was built.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d separate their contributions. DiT asks a very basic question: do diffusion models need to be built around a U-Net, or can a fairly standard Transformer work just as well? The important result is that you can replace that backbone with a Transformer operating on latent patches, and get a model whose quality improves predictably as you scale compute. To me, that makes DiT useful beyond any particular benchmark: it gives generative modeling a simple architecture that people can build on.

SiT keeps much of that architecture and looks at the modeling framework around it. How do you connect data and noise? What do you ask the network to predict? How do you sample from the learned process? Through stochastic interpolants, it provides a way to study those choices together, including diffusion and flow-based formulations.

So I see them as complementary. DiT establishes the Transformer backbone; SiT explores how to train and sample that backbone more effectively. I wouldn’t attribute SiT’s gains to a new architecture—the interesting contribution is showing how much those other design choices matter.

r001.rationale: The response presents DiT as a useful architecture people can build on and SiT as exploring training and sampling choices, but does not characterize them as academic baselines or say subsequent research was built on them.
